title: Improvement Exchange Planning
name: Improvement Exchange Planning
metaTitle: Improvement Exchange Planning in Dallas, TX
metaDescription: Planning a build-to-suit or improvement 1031 exchange for Dallas investors, using an exchange accommodation titleholder to fund construction within 180 days.

sections.html: Sometimes the ideal replacement property for a Dallas exchange does not exist yet in its finished, ready-to-use form, a parcel needs a building, or an existing building needs enough work done to match the relinquished property's value. An improvement exchange lets exchange proceeds fund that construction, but the entire scope has to close within the same 180-day window every other exchange runs on, which changes how the planning has to work from day one. Construction and tax deadlines rarely move at the same speed, and reconciling the two is the central challenge of this structure, one that has to be solved before ground is ever broken rather than worked out as delays come up.

sections.heading: Why the Property Cannot Simply Be Titled Directly to the Exchanger During Construction
sections.html: If the investor took title to the replacement property directly while improvements were still underway, only the value that exists at the time of transfer would count toward the exchange, not whatever the property is worth once finished. Improvement exchanges solve this by having an exchange accommodation titleholder, a special entity set up for this purpose, hold title while construction happens and exchange funds pay for the work. The property transfers to the investor only once improvements are complete enough to reflect the intended exchange value, still inside the 180-day period. Setting up the titleholder entity itself takes time and coordination with the qualified intermediary, so this decision needs to be made early rather than added on partway through a construction timeline already underway.

sections.heading: Why 180 Days Is Such a Tight Window for Real Construction Work
sections.html: Ground-up construction rarely finishes in 180 days, which means improvement exchanges usually apply to a parcel with an existing structure needing renovation or expansion, rather than a from-scratch build. A Dallas investor targeting a South Dallas industrial building that needs dock door additions or an office suite near Preston Center needing a buildout has a realistic shot at finishing within the window; a ground-up warehouse development typically does not, unless it was already well underway before the exchange began. Matching the scope of work to the days actually available is the first filter that rules candidates in or out, well before price or location become the deciding factors. A realistic contractor estimate, checked against permitting timelines specific to the jurisdiction the property sits in, should come before any exchange accommodation titleholder arrangement gets set up, since the whole structure only makes sense if the schedule is genuinely achievable.

sections.heading: What Has to Be Locked In Before Construction Starts
sections.html: Because the exchange accommodation titleholder is the party actually contracting for construction, the scope of work, budget, and contractor need to be settled early enough that the arrangement holds up as a genuine improvement exchange rather than an informal side agreement. Change orders, cost overruns, or delays discovered mid-construction are harder to absorb here than in a typical renovation project, since every added week comes directly out of the same 180 days the rest of the exchange depends on. Building in a contingency buffer against the construction schedule, rather than planning to the exact number of days available, is what keeps a normal permitting delay from turning into a failed exchange.

sections.heading: What Planning Covers From Identification Through Transfer
sections.html:
An improvement exchange plan generally tracks:

  • Selection and engagement of an exchange accommodation titleholder before any construction contract is signed
  • Written identification of the property and the improvements as part of the 45-day notice
  • Construction budget and schedule confirmed against the remaining days in the 180-day window
  • Draw schedule for exchange funds paid to contractors through the titleholder
  • Final transfer of title to the investor once improvements are complete enough to count

sections.heading: Where This Fits Against Simpler Exchange Structures
sections.html: Improvement exchanges cost more to run than a straightforward forward exchange, since they involve setting up and maintaining the titleholder entity for the duration of construction. They earn that cost when the best available Dallas replacement genuinely needs work to match the relinquished property's value, and a plain purchase of an as-is property would leave value on the table or force the investor into a lesser asset just to hit the deadline. Weighing that tradeoff honestly, before committing to the added complexity, is worth doing early rather than midway through a construction timeline that is already running.

faqs.q: Who actually owns the property while it is being improved?
faqs.a: The exchange accommodation titleholder, a separate entity set up specifically to hold title during the improvement period, holds the property until construction is complete enough to transfer to the investor within the 180-day window.

faqs.q: Can I use an improvement exchange for a ground-up building?
faqs.a: It is possible but difficult, since ground-up construction rarely finishes within 180 days. Improvement exchanges more commonly apply to renovation, expansion, or buildout work on an existing structure that can realistically be completed in the available time.

faqs.q: What happens if construction is not finished by day 180?
faqs.a: Only the value of improvements actually completed and in place by the transfer date counts toward the exchange. Unfinished work at day 180 does not carry forward, which is why realistic scheduling before construction starts matters more here than in most renovation projects.

faqs.q: Does this structure cost more to set up than a standard exchange?
faqs.a: Yes, generally. Establishing and maintaining the exchange accommodation titleholder entity, along with the added coordination between construction and the exchange timeline, adds cost compared to a straightforward forward exchange into an as-is property.
